text: Synthesis for article drafting: Evidence consistently identifies "The Rector of Justin" as a 1964 novel by Louis Auchincloss, not a play by Philip Barry. The book is set at Justin Martyr, an elite New England boys' boarding school founded and led by aging headmaster (rector) Francis Prescott. The story is framed through Hugh Carver, a young teacher and clergyman who is writing Prescott's biography, and through additional narrative voices that complicate Prescott's public image.[1][2][3] Plot and thematic discussions describe the novel as following Prescott late in his career as he faces retirement, institutional politics, and revelations about his past, including tensions within his family and questions about his ambition and use of power in building the school.[2][4] Critics and teachers note that the novel explores themes of moral authority, religious conviction, the ethics of educational leadership, social class, and the gap between public reputation and private character, and it is often grouped with American "campus" or "school" novels.[2][3][4] Publication records from 1964 and later editions confirm its status as a work of fiction and one of Auchincloss's better-known novels, which has continued to appear on reading lists and in scholarship on American education and campus fiction.[1][3] This synthesis can ground the lead, plot summary, themes, and publication/reception sections of a Wikipedia-style article, while the misattribution to Philip Barry should be addressed briefly in a background or attribution note rather than treating the book as Barry's play.

title: Background and authorship

A related Library of Congress contributor biography, prepared for Auchinclosss novel The Education of Oscar Fairfax, states that he "has written more than sixty books" and explicitly lists The Rector of Justin among his novels. WorldCats union catalog record for The rector of Justin (OCLC 5751292) similarly describes the work as a novel by Auchincloss, clustering multiple printings and editions under the same author and title. [16][17][18][15]

Publisher-oriented materials and institutional summaries of Auchinclosss career describe him as a Wall Street lawyer and prolific novelist whose first novel, The Indifferent Children, appeared in 1947, and they list The Rector of Justin among his notable later works. An American Library in Paris newsletter notes that Auchincloss had "a successful career as a Wall Street lawyer" while producing numerous books, including The Rector of Justin, reinforcing its status as part of his ongoing exploration of upper-class American institutions. [32][19]

Research into Philip Barrys bibliography and archival holdings shows no record of a play titled The Rector of Justin in his body of work. Biographical entries and reference summaries of Barrys career list plays such as Paris Bound, Holiday, and The Philadelphia Story, but do not mention a work by this title. title: Plot
content:

Commentary on the novel describes Prescott as a towering public figure at the school whose reputation and myth have been built over decades of leadership, while the narrative gradually reveals his more complex inner life and the frailties behind his authoritative image. [2][16][30][8]

Plot-focused discussion from a literary blog summarizes an important strand of the story through the character Brian Aspinwall, who becomes a teacher at age twenty-seven at the prestigious New England school after being suddenly recruited. Aspinwalls arrival provides a younger perspective on the institution and its rector, enabling readers to see the schools traditions and Prescotts leadership through the eyes of a newcomer whose admiration and doubts evolve over time. [36][30]

Critical summaries emphasize that the narrative unfolds through a series of viewpoints, each adding layers to the portrayal of Prescott and the school; this structure underscores how different observers construct and deconstruct his reputation. As these voices revisit key episodes in the schools history and in Prescotts personal life, including his family relationships and religious commitments, the plot moves toward a portrait of an institutional leader confronting his legacy and the divergence between his ideals and their realization. [8][30][29]
